node.label: Julie Cruikshank
node.date_label: Life Lived Like a Story, collaborative (1990) · The Social Life of Stories (1998) · Do Glaciers Listen? (2005)
node.description: Julie Cruikshank’s The Social Life of Stories (1998) explores the social power of storytelling and how it can mediate between social action and local knowledge. In Do Glaciers Listen? (2005), she argues that local knowledge is made through encounters and she treats environmental change, local knowledge and colonial encounters as connected themes. Life Lived Like a Story (1990) was produced through collaboration between Julie Cruikshank, Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned. Innes explicitly used her flexible account of oral history and oral tradition alongside Angela Cavender-Wilson’s in his 1999–2000 methodological article. Cole Harris praised Do Glaciers Listen? as a grounded interdisciplinary achievement but questioned its handling of scientific explanation and asked her to address communication between knowledge systems more directly (2005/06). Dorothee Schreiber challenged Harris’s framing in a published response (2008).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Life Lived Like a Story: Life Stories of Three Yukon Native Elders (1990), in collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned; Reading Voices: Dän Dhá Ts’edenintth’ę (1991); The Social Life of Stories: Narrative and Knowledge in the Yukon Territory (1998); Do Glaciers Listen? Local Knowledge, Colonial Encounters, and Social Imagination (2005; anniversary edition, foreword by Paul Nadasdy, 2026).
node.scope_note: Selected methodological passages read in the 1993 draft, 1997 and 2001 articles, and 2005 publisher-sample introduction; selected Innes (1999–2000) and Schreiber (2008) passages and Harris’s four-page review read. The 1990, 1991 and 1998 books, remaining 2005 chapters, 1994 Canadian Historical Review article, 2026 foreword and cited theorists’ originals remain unread; book claims otherwise use publisher descriptions.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Social Life of Stories (1998), as its publisher describes it, draws on Walter Benjamin’s insights on storytelling and dialogue.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UBC Press description of The Social Life of Stories (1998), which names 'the insights of Walter Benjamin, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Harold Innis'. The 1997 American Anthropologist article was not read on a recorded permitted route, so no page locators are used. Benjamin's own work unread; no personal contact asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Glaciers and Climate Change” (2001), Cruikshank follows Latour’s proposal that scientific research should address uncertainty rather than promise to end controversy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary discussion pp. 389–390 and conclusion p. 391: “Following Latour’s advice”; reference p. 392 names From the World of Science to the World of Research (1998). Latour’s original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Do Glaciers Listen? (2005) in 2005/06, Cole Harris praises its interdisciplinary achievement but challenges its treatment of scientific explanation and asks Cruikshank to address communication across knowledge systems more squarely.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Harris review pp. 104–106 read: praise p. 104, scales/explanatory objection p. 105, final request p. 106, “address this problem of communication more squarely”. A qualified criticism; not a wholesale dismissal. Book read only in selected introduction passages.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Oral History Methods in Native Studies” (1999–2000), Innes adopts Cruikshank’s flexible account of oral history and oral tradition, alongside Angela Cavender-Wilson’s, as useful for interpreting his interviews.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Innes pp. 65–67, nn. 8–14, read in Saskatchewan institutional PDF. Calls the two scholars’ conception “operational” (p. 67); cites Cruikshank’s 1993 draft and Life Lived Like a Story (1990). Shared credit retained. Interview narratives excluded; books unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Claiming Legitimacy: Oral Tradition and Oral History (1993 draft), Cruikshank asks historians to examine how oral traditions are used in the present rather than treat them as fixed stores of recoverable facts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary draft pp. 1–3 and 7–9 read: “how oral tradition is used” (p. 2). A methodological proposal, not adopted Commission policy. Distinct from the collective Life Lived Like a Story routes (edges 2173–2175 and 750); no new authorship claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Glaciers and Climate Change” (2001), Cruikshank brings historical interpretation to climate debates and argues that local knowledge must be understood within the political histories that shape it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary abstract p. 377 and discussion pp. 390–391 read: knowledge cannot be “ahistorical, timeless, abstract data” (p. 390). Method and policy argument only; no community knowledge reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Do Glaciers Listen? (2005), Cruikshank connects social memory with environmental history by asking how changing landscapes help people interpret changing historical circumstances.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary introduction pp. 11–12: fourth theme names “memory, stability, and change”; distinguishes changing landscapes from static archives of remembrance. Other chapters unread. UBC research statement explicitly links memory and environmental anthropology.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1999 review essay, Franca Iacovetta favourably reviews Life Lived Like a Story (1990), made by Julie Cruikshank in collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned, preferring its restrained authorial presence to Ruth Behar’s in Translated Woman (1993).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Iacovetta’s substantive comparison and surrounding methodological discussion. This records favourable reception, not a demonstrated influence on her earlier monograph. Cruikshank’s book was not read. Review comparisons are undirected under Task O.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Life Lived Like a Story (1990), Julie Cruikshank’s collaboration with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned offered a model of ethnography that foregrounded the collaborators’ voices, as Wendy Wickwire’s 1993 review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Wickwire’s evaluation of collaboration and authorial restraint as a change in ethnographic practice. This is a methodological contribution supported by a review; the book itself remains unread. The original year is confirmed in Iacovetta, p. 289, note 23.
